The point is, though, that none of the NCL players here are really
advocating simply playing 6 cards in a game. If that's what you did,
then it's no wonder you found the games boring. The thing about NCL is
that it *allows* you to have more than 4 of each card in a deck - it
does not force you. Cards like Bewitching Oration become more useful
because you can have enough of them in the deck to rely on them - making
something like a Setite vote deck much more possible (since the Setites
don't really have any real voting power from their vampires - a couple
with 2 votes each, I believe). And Corruption becomes viable as well.
With only 4 in a deck, you're screwed because you'll find it a hard job
to get all 4 out of the deck most likely and you'll only be stealing
someone like, say, Gideon Fontaine, Roman Alexander or someone like
that. But the other cards are yours to do what you will with. In a
Ventrue vote deck, you might have quite a few Bewitching Orations,
Conservative Agitations and Kine Resources Contested (multiples of each)
but then you can do what you like. Do you want to have a few Elder
Kindred Networks in there, just to put off other people calling votes?
Maybe an Island of Yiaros or two. Have to defend your vampires so a few
Majesties or Catatonic Fears might do the trick, or do you want to go
for the slightly more difficult to pull off (when you only have 2 or 3
of each card in your deck) Skin of Steel with Pulled Fangs cheese?
Well, there's always a couple of Hunting Ground cards in there - and you
could have a couple of things like the Traditions to spice up the game a
little. A few Dramatic Upheavals or Kindred Restructures will annoy a
few people too. As prayer cards, you might like to consider Peace
Treaty or Disputed Territory, and Praxis Solomon might help you bargain
with a few people in the middle of them contesting each other.

So, yes, you might have, say, 10 Bewitching Orations, 10 KRC and 10 Con
Agi to allow you to have a solid, workable strategy, but with the other
40, 50, 60 or however many cards you've got left, you can go to town and
have some fun and allow other strategies to develop. I mean, with your
Ventrue, you can maybe drop a little bleed in there - doubling up as
either transfers (GtU and Scouting Mission) or location stealing
(Dominate Kine).

Bill wrote:
"One day, we switched over to 4CL. It was a whole new game, and it was
infinitely better."

What made it infinitely better?

"I must agree that it got kinda old playing the same 6 or so cards 10 times in
a game."

If you were only playing with 6 cards, you were playing a very different game
than most of the rest of us. NL alows you to build a deck to any possible
specifications to do what you need to do. It does not make you play decks that
have 15 copies each of 6 different cards.

As an aside, in all of these recent 4CL/NL debates, the 4CL folks keep bringing
up that the game is "more fun" because 4CL menas that you don't see the same
cards over and over. I don't know about the rest of you, but I play Jyhad for
the rich and varied strategic interactions between decks in a game, not to see
all the cards. I have all the cards. I've seen all the cards. If I want to
get a thrill out of seeing lots of different cards, I'll look in my boxes. The
different pictures on the different cards are not what makes Jyhad an exiting
game. It is the complex interaction between decks in a game. It is "What
happens when a close range Rush deck sits between a weenie vote deck and a Fast
Reaction Tremere Intercept deck?", not "Ooh! This time he played a
Conditioning! Last time he played a Threats! Cool!".

"IMO, 4CL forces you to actually think about what you want your deck to do and
how to go about making that possible... if you want a, well, not brainless, but
less thought-provoking game, play NCL or Doom or something. 4CL makes for a
much better game."

Ok, now this statement is just insane. Sure. You like 4CL because it makes
all the decks less focused. Sure. You like 4CL cause it makes everyone use
lots of different cards. Ok. You like 4Cl cause it slows the game down some.
Alright. You like 4CL cause you don't have to figure out how to deal with deck
that have 15 Majesties. Whatever. To state that 4CL makes Jyhad, a brilliant
game that was specifically designed to _not_ have card limits a _better_ game
than the designers intended is sheer lunacy. How does 4CL make the game more
thought provoking? By limiting your options? By insuring that all 4CL decks
will have exactly 4 of all the useful cards? By making the most important
skill in deck construction to be "how do I get around the 4CL"? By completely
nullifying the importance of the subtle differences between cards like Skin of
Steel and Superior Mettle?

Sure, you may like 4CL better than NL. By all means, go ahead. It certainly
does not make it a _better_ game.

Please don't take any of these comments as a personal afront. I'm glad you are
here on the newsgroup, posting about and playing Jyhad. Please stay. Argue
all you want. I'm just always like this.

Eric wrote:
"I mean if you put 15 conditioning with 15 lost in crowds do the other cards in
the deck really matter all that much??"

This argument is completely pointless as a defense of 4CL. How is 15
Conditioning and 15 Lost in Crowds in any way strategically different than 4
Govern/4Conditioning/4 Bonding/4Threats with 4Lost/4Cloak/4Faceless/4Mask?
There is no strategic difference, only subtle tactical difference that gets
lost under the yoke of 4CL. Ok, perhaps you like 4CL because it makes people
use all the different cards, but the strategic difference between these two
examples are completely negligible, and consequently in no way a viable defense
of 4CL as requiring "More creative decks".

"no its just this turn I had the blood to spend last turn I didn'tbut since
vampires don't run out of blood in NL They only use conditioning. :-)-~"

And so this turn your deck doesn't work when last turn it did. If you have a
deck that worries about running out of blood in NL, you use more Threats than
Conditioning. If you don't care about blood costs, you use more Conditioning
than Threats. Under 4CL, you just use 4 of each.

"This is a misconception you have about us at least me anyway.We did not
instate a rule just so we could figure out how to get
around it."

You stated yourself in posts about Rush decks that Sports Bikes were a more
reliable way to get into combat. That seems like trying to get around the lack
of available Bum's Rushes to me.

"how so? could it not be said that NL players make a choice on a card based

on...well hypothetical situations. while I might use 2 of each and make the
choice of which to play based on a real in game situation."

Sure, ok. If you decide that you only need 4 damage prevention cards in your
deck, and you chose to use 3 Skin of Steel and 1 Superior Mettle for pure
design reasons, then I grant you that. More often then not, however, under 4CL
the two different cards just mean that you get to use 4 Skin of Steel and 4
Superior Mettle, effectively just getting around the limit on Skin of Steel.
Under NL, a deck designer will have to make a specific choice between weither
he wants to stop multiple strikes in one round, or stop strikes from pressed
rounds of combat. Under 4CL, you just use 4 of each.

The same goes for Obfuscate cards. Under NL, the differences between Lost in
Crowds, Cloak the Gathering, and Faceless Night have specific meaning. Under
4CL, they don't, they are just more stealth cards that allow you to get around
the 4CL. I just built a deck tonight, and decided that I had room for 9 cards
that gave me stealth. I, for very specific reasons, chose to use 9 Cloak the
Gathering. The Cloaks are much more useful than Lost or Faceless would be in
this deck, so I used all Cloaks. Under 4CL, I would not have this choice. I
would use 4 Cloak, 4 Lost, and one of something else, which would still work
more or less, but would lose the tactical depth of the different card effects.

"of course you'll argue that mine are not as reliable but since thats not my
only option I'll more than likely be able to deal with whatever comes at me
While your screwed if you didn't account for something while you were building
your deck."

You seem to keep missing the concept that focused decks do not become screwed

by things that were not accounted for when building them. When building a good
deck, you need to consider all possible angles--"How will S+B affect me? How
will Fortitude affect me? How will Rush combat affect me? How will offensive
voting affect me?" All decks will have weaknessess, and the only thing you can
do about it is plan for them with your strategy. Focused decks win by virtue
of their strength and reliability. Diverse decks die by virtue of not being
reliable and not being able to respond to any particular threat in a consistent
manner.

Peter D Bakija

I've been playing Jyhad for about 3 or 4 years on a deck drawn from no more
than a conglomeration of 5 or so starter decks and no more than a handful of
boosters. With only a small bunch of fellow Jyhad players to trade with, and
no tournaments to speak of out here in the backwaters of Ireland, our group
hasn't had much choice about playing 4cl or not (with the odd exception -- 5
deer rifles instead of 4). Now that Wizards has decided to put an end to
V:tES we've all decided to indulge our passion and go ahead and waste our
savings on boxes and boxes of boosters. So for the first time we can
construct the decks of our dreams. If we want to throw in 5 dawn operations
we actually can. As you can imagine, this is fairly exciting: we're now
playing the real V:tES, we're able to pursue tangible strategies that yield
results fairly rapidly. It really adds an extra dimension to our whole game.
The spendthrift player is no longer the one who wins -- it's the skilful
player. But of course, as is evident from a quick browse of posts on this
newsgroup, there are only a limited number of straightahead deck strategies
to choose from: Brujah rush, Ventrue vote-to-death, Malk sneak and bleed,
aggravated, etc.etc. I'm sure we'll all tire fairly quickly of playing
super-tuned decks comprised of only an harmonic few cards. Yeah, your right
I guess, varied decks are most entertaining. The varied, unfocused,
well-played deck that's stood the test of time will be the one you turn to
at the end of the day, when that novelty has worn off. But do appreciate the
desire to indulge your dreams by putting together such a focused deck,
especially when it's been a dream for so damn long, or more especially when
it still is a dream. I guess that's why focused decks are referred to as
"munchie" decks.
Richard

Generally, my NL decks have a concept that they are based around. My Ventrue
bruise&bleed is based around doing big bleeds(6 GtU, 5 Conditioning, 4
Threats). If I get blocked, my usual strategy is to Trap them and hit them
for a little damage each round(6 Traps, 6 Superior Mettle, various other
fortitude prevention, and a few weapons). There are 2 Ivory Bows, since they
can let the combat get over quicker. In the case where my vamps are low on
blood, I'll bleed and use Trap and then Undead Persistance to take them down
with me (this works because it has very low cap vampires in it. All less than
7 and a couple of 1's and 2's). The deck is, admittedly, a fun deck, but in

unfortunately, waste me every time. Other than that, it's only weakness is
against focused non-combat decks, which are frowned upon here. 8)
I guess in this situation the non-combat deck stigmata is to my advantage.

wouldn't have my Traps. But I still don't really have more than 6 or 7 of any

under 4CL. Really the only difference between it and a 4CL deck is that I
have 2 extra traps, I used an extra Conditioning instead of, say,
Foreshadowing Destruction, I used 2 extra GtU's instead of Scouting Mission,

3 Skin's of Steel I think) or Rolling With the Punches (2 of these, I think).

really aren't as one-dimensional single-combo oriented as you seem to imply.

abusive decks, while not giving the possibilities of strange decks. My
Bauble/Assault Rifle/Daring the Dawn/Possession deck is not at all possible
under 4CL. It's weak even under NL, but it's still possible. So, why is

each playgroup should choose for itself, that's not really under contention.

But that is an incorrect assessment of the situation. The decks that are
brought up most often on this group, i.e. the ones you mention above, are
brought up because they are easily identifiable and understandable archtypes,
and consequently make for easy disccussion. I don't really need to explain
what a Brujah Rush deck does or a Malk S+B deck for them to be used as a
example in a debate. Other decks, however, are not so easily envisioned, and
thus don't make good ammo for strategy disscussion. It is much easier to
describe a Ventrue Vote Deck in three words than it is to explain a
Malk/Gangrel/Lasombra Obf/Dom/Pro Form of Mist/Obediance/Bonding deck in 12
words, but both decks are prefectly viable and sucessful under NL. The Ventrue
Deck gets alot more air time just because it is a much easier example.

The strength of No Limit Jyhad is that there are literally an infinite number
of decks that you can build, and most of them are pretty competetive. Under
4CL, the best Malk S+B deck is probably the best deck you can make, and will
always dominate the play enviornment, requiring game circles to "Shame" players
out of using the Malkavian S+B deck ("Yeah. Real clever, Stealth and Bleed
boy..."). Under NL, there is no need for this, as any number of weird or
archtypical decks can easily compete with such a Malk deck. Under 4CL, for
instance, you can't build a Nosferatu deck that relies solely on Behind You
(the only good Obf manuver available) for manuvering, as you can only use 4.
Under 4CL, you can't build an Animalism deck that makes extensive use out of
Aid From Bats, as you can only have 4 of them. Under NL, however, both of
these weird deck concepts are perfectly viable and, when used in a well
designed deck, can easily compete with the best archtype decks.

I assure you that by playing with No Card Limits, and by pushing yourselves,
your decks will never grow stagnant. I play Jyhad a great deal, and change my
decks all the time. Currently I have a Pot/Obf Nosferatu Rush deck, a Wennie
Pro untap/intercept/bleed deck, an Ani/Obf intercept/light combat/bleed deck,
and a Obf/Pre spawning 3rd tradition pool gain deck. All of these are farily
successful, completely competetive, and certainly not archtypical.

and most of all Atonement. This card really rocks. With the untap
potential of the Gangrel and the low capacity you should be able to
block any attempts to harm you or your cards in play by turn 3 or 4.

My own personal feelings on the whole No-Limit[NL] vs X Card-limit
things:

I get bored playing a deck that has many many duplicates of any
given card (say, 8 or more). If the game's going to go on for a while,
there needs to be some variety to keep my interest. Even in a NL
evironment, I doubt I'd ever include more than 10 cards that were
functionally equivalent, or more than 6-8 of a single card, just
because of my own personal preference for variety in a deck.

This puts me at a potential disadvantage if going against NL decks.
I prefer a game where I have a fair shot at winning, and so I prefer
playing in an environment with card limits. An additional reason
for this is that I don't like the game-play to get repetitive -
even if my deck has variety and surprises, if my predator or
prey is doing the same thing, with the same cards, every turn,
again the game gets dull IMHO. If others are abiding by some card
limits, this is less likely to happen.

All that said, I think the 4 card limit is too small. It's just too
restrictive on some strategies, and on generically useful cards like
WakeWEF. I played a game with a group that used a 6 limit, and I think
that works quite nicely.

As far as the gentleman's agreements to avoid having the table swept
by the Stealth/Bleed decks, to me it's more a matter of finding
a playgroup composed of people imaginative enough that it's not
a concern. Even the stealth/bleed thing can be made interesting by
adding in some wacky Malkavian randomness and other surprises. If
one of my opponents won't even bother doing that much, I'm not
interested in playing with them anymore.

Wait, wait, wait. What if someone _wants_ to play a stealth and bleed

That restriction being: "the deck doesn't have to be too effective"?
How is this playing to win? You can make goofy decks, and they'll
probably get trounced upon the first few times you play them, but you
can make basically any deck effective with some practice and good
deckbuilding skills. You don't have to impose an articifical "no S&B"
rule.

> next game.

But "the Malks", or any sleath/bleed, or _any_ effecitive bleed deck is
just another deck in NL. If you don't want to put Bleed defense or Vote
defense into your decks, and then shame people out of using bleed and
vote decks, then you're not really playing Jyhad. You're playing some
sort of meta-Jyhad.

> and then after we lose to it, ask the player to switch decks for the
> next game. It's nice to be reminded once in a while of the power of brainless
> decks, and then to get on with the real Jyhad.

The thing that I don't think you realize is that the brainless decks
(like, for example, straight dom/obf S&B) are NOT VERY EFFECTIVE. (sorry
to shout)

Example: in Crusade:Ithaca a few weeks back, there was a straight
Malkavian stealth/bleed deck. It got NO victory points the entire
tournament. Why? Because the other decks had bleed defense. And this
deck was not well enough constructed (I gathered the deck-owner was a
new player) to handle this, and it died.

THIS is the real Jyhad.

When the Ithaca group, which I was until recently a part of, switched to
NL, we had the same kind of problem. We build very, very narrow decks,
without bleed or vote defenses, because nobody really liked playing
those kind of decks. Hence we all played combat decks, and we evolved
amazingly vicious combat decks.

But when anyone would come by with a Ventrue bleed deck (with Skin of
Steels and Bondings, natch), they'd sweep the table in a matter of
minutes. The weenie vote and bleed decks would also sweep regularly.
In many ways, our group was like what you describe.

So what changed? We realized that we were just like we had been in our
4CL days, shaming people out of playing effective decks that we didn't
know how to deal with. So we decided to start keeping score. We used
the Corrupter's scoring system (I won't get into detail here), and
started "playing to win".

Suddenly, it was OK to play your vote deck, or your bleed deck. Once
people got tired of losing to them, we learned to put in defenses, and
our games got much more interesting because now we all had lots of
different decks. People who had only made combat decks made killer
bleed decks and had fun with them. Contrary to popular belief, some
people enjoy playing effective stealth and bleed decks.
If you peruse the deck archives, you'll find that I myself had an
effective obf/pre deck. It won a lot, and was a lot of fun to play.

But the deck didn't need to be ganged up on, either. Why should someone
across the table deal with a deck just because it's a S&B deck? "Let
_them_ deal with it! I'm busy ousting my own prey."

Moral of the story: the game has ways to keep stealth/bleed under
control. It doesn't need your help or extra unspoken rules (other than
GT, natch) to make it work better.

That's my rant for the day. :)

James

Well, I don't know. The winning deck from the recent Portsmouth
tournament was made under the (misguided) impression that he had to be
working to a 5CL. It won.

For many of us, the point about NCL vs 4CL is partly competitive. If I
want to make an out and out combat deck, I should be allowed to. NCL
allows me to make an out and out combat deck the way *I* want to. It
doesn't force me to use Sport Bikes instead of Rush but I still have the
option to do so IF I WANT. 4CL does have a little more of a tendency to
homogonise some deck types because you run out of the cards you want to
use and then have to use the other cards to replace them.

And choice is the other major factor. Some discussions at Portsmouth
basically boiled down to the following points:

1) NCL does allow you to play a hideously focussed deck strategy
2) If you're not very lucky, a very focussed deck won't do too well on
its own - you need the diversification
3) However, 4CL virtually forces you to diversify which, though it
should make for a better deck, doesn't *necessarily* do so
4) Though the need to diversify is there, surely I should be allowed to
have as many of some cards as I like in a deck

A real life example I don't think I've dragged out before is the way *I*
play Gangrel decks. Of course, I like to have Claw cards in the deck -
both Wolf and Claws of the Dead. However, I much prefer to have more
Claws of the Dead in the deck since they CAN double up as maneuvers. I
like to have a couple of Wolf Claws there to provide me the flexibility
to press, of course (although I'm using, say, Gleam of Red Eyes and Form
of the Ghost for both of these as necessary) but I just like Claws of
the Dead better. I personally think I should have the choice to do what
I want with the deck and not be forced, if I want claws, to have 4 of
each - I'd rather have 6 to 8 Claws of the Dead and only a couple of
Wolf Claws. And I can do other things with the deck - Damage
Prevention, Animalism untap maybe, Shackles of Inky-Doo, a few of the
really cool retainers etc. etc. etc. But for my combat section of the
deck, I like to have full control over what I do with it.

Well, it can be a hell of a difference. In this instance, Staredown
only dodges at inferior - you can get panned on the additional strikes
if someone's playing a nasty deck.

But there are many other instances where the difference between two
cards is more pronounced. What do I care more about doing? Untapping
or dealing damage? In that case, Catatonic Fear versus Majesty is a
real decision. Do I want to tap their vampires to prevent them blocking
actions later in the turn or would I prefer the ability to get extra
stealth on my actions from other vampires? In that case, Cloak the
Gathering versus Faceless Night is a real decision.

In many cases, it waits until you get the superior version of a card
(rather than inferior) and then you have to start making decisions as to
which is "better" for the type of deck you want to play.

The thing I love about NCL is that, yes, you can play archetypal decks

else you can do. Corruption is viable. Votes passed with Bribes, not

using 3rd Tradition and pool gain using Consanguineous Boon is possible

ways that would normally be prohibitively expensive pool wise, using

gives you the flexibility to NOT do so if you CHOOSE not to do so.

entirely.
